SUE Design Manager User Guide

Chapter 7

The SUE Programming Interface

The SUE Programming Interface

SUE provides a simple programming interface or API for changing cells, modifying cells, accessing cell contents, printing cells, adding menu commands, etc. from Tcl. This interface consists of Tcl-accessible procedures which complement the list of SUE global variables listed in the .suerc files and in the Text commands/variables menu item in the Help menu. Simple applications, like netlisting all SUE schematics in a given directory, should be very easy to accomplish through this interface. This is a new interface, so it is probably incomplete.

SUE uses certain Tcl global variables and procedures. If you write Tcl programs that stomp on these variables or procedures, you are likely to cause unexpected problems.

Do not use any undocumented SUE Tcl procedures that you may find or have heard about. These procedures are likely to leave SUE in an inconsistent state. Furthermore, they are likely to change in future versions of SUE.

SUE commands and variables are further documented online under Text commands/variables in the Help menu. This command creates a popup window to display documentation about specific commands and global variables. The list of commands and variables can further be filtered by keyword and printed. The online documentation is more complete than this manual.

Tcl procedures can be executed from SUE by typing them into the window from which SUE was started (i.e., the SUE command window), which is a Tcl interpreter. All top-level Tcl procedures that execute SUE API calls should be wrapped with the launch procedure instead of being executed directly. While commands will still work otherwise, they will be slower, especially if they switch the current cell using api_goto_cell, api_push, api_pop, api_load_cell, or api_new_cell.

Procedures called from the menu or hotkeys and added using the menu_add command automatically get wrapped with the launch procedure.

The launch command also adds error catching. If a Tcl error occurs in a user procedure, the stack trace is placed in the error global variable.

Alternatively, procedures can be called from UNIX by placing them in the SUE command line using the syntax described earlier. For example, the following line: 

      sue foo.sue -CMD api_netlist -CMD exit -ICONIFY 1 -BATCH 1 
     

will load the schematic foo.sue, netlist it, and then exit. By setting -BATCH 1, SUE will bypass asking for confirmation on any operations. These commands are automatically wrapped with launch. Lastly, commands can be added to the SUE menus with the menu_add command as described below.

Only simple SUE procedures can be called from the command line interface, i.e. you cannot send a list to -CMD or -SET. This is a shell limitation. If you want to execute a procedure at startup that requires arguments, you need to define a wrapper procedure that takes no arguments and calls the desired procedure with the appropriate arguments, possibly using global variables that can be set on the command line.

User-defined procedures can either be added to the .suerc file or placed in a file with the suffix .tcl. All procedures in the auto-search path in .tcl files will be automatically loaded when needed.

If you want to execute a command, such as a SUE API call, at startup, you can either specify it on the SUE startup line as described above or add it to the SUE_EXECUTE variable in the .suerc file. API commands cannot be executed directly from .suerc files sinces SUE is not yet initialized at that point. Any commands contained in SUE_EXECUTE will get executed after SUE comes up but before any command-line commands get executed.

For simplicity, you should use the TCL lappend command to add commands to SUE_EXECUTE. To set the listboxes at startup, add the following lines to your local .suerc file: 

      lappend SUE_EXECUTE \ 
"api_icon_listbox -command change -dir $SUE_DIR/schematics/devices -index 1" 
       
      lappend SUE_EXECUTE \ 
"api_icon_listbox -command change -dir $SUE_DIR/schematics/mspice -index 2"


SUE cannot execute without an X window, even if you never want to see it (this is a TK thing). The best you can do is iconify the window with "-ICONIFY 1". However, you still need to run on a system that has X running on it.

The following sections describe all of the additional Tcl procedures that are available for use in programming. These procedures and variables can also be found in Text Commands/Variables in the Help menu in SUE.

SUE API Procedures

All of the SUE API procedures are described in the Micro Magic Tools SUE API Reference Manual.

In addition, the most current documentation of the SUE API commands and varaibles can be viewed with the Text Commands/Variables command in the Help menu.

Generic Procedures

In addition to all of the standard Tcl built-in procedures, SUE provides the following generic procedures that you can use when programming inside of SUE:

get_assoc <name> <list>

Returns the value associated with <name> in the given associative list, or nil if no value exists.

Example: 

      sue> get_assoc foo {{bar 3} {foo 5}} 
      
      5
min <num> [<num> ...]
max <num> [<num> ...]

Returns the min/max number of the list of numbers.

Example: 

      sue> min 23.4 65.5 12.3 
      
      12.3
pp_number <num> [<format "%g%s">]

Pretty prints a number using the spice metric suffixes (metric prefixes), for example: G=109 (giga), M=106 (mega), K=103 (kilo), m=10-3 (milli), u=10-6 (micro), n=10-9 (nano), p=10-12 (pico), f=10-15 (femto), a=10-18 (atto).

Example: 

      sue> pp_number 23.4e-7 
      
      2.34u
parse_pp_number <string>

Parses a string with spice notation (see pp_number, above) into a computer-readable number. Trailing units are ignored. Examples of valid input strings are: 3.2e-4, 32.4fF, 23 Ohms.

Example: 

      sue> parse_pp_number 32.4fF 
      
      3.24e-14
setl <var_list> &ltlist>

Sets each variable in <var_list> in the current context to the nth argument in <list>.

Example: 

      setl {x y} $foo 
     

is equivalent to, but syntactically nicer than: 

      set x [lindex $foo 0] 
      set y [lindex $foo 1]
use_first <var_list>

Evaluates variables in <var_list> in the current context in order. If the variable is defined and non-nil, returns its value. If none are defined, returns nil (""). Constants can be added using the syntax <constant>.

Example: 

      sue> set b 23 
      sue> use_first a b c 
      23 
      sue> use_first aa bb cc '58 
      58

SUE-Specific Procedures

SUE also provides certain SUE-specific procedures. These procedures are not API procedures; in other words, they do not query or change the SUE database, but are specific to SUE as explained:

bus_expand <name>

Expands <name> into a list of all of its bits and returns it if it is a bus, otherwise just returns it. Only understands SUE bus notation.

Example: 

      sue> bus_expand {foo[3:0]} 
      foo[0] foo[1] foo[2] foo[3] 
      sue> bus_expand bar 
      bar
bus_width <name>

Returns the bus width of <name>. Only understands SUE bus notation.

Example: 

      sue> bus_width {foo[3:0]} 
      4 
      sue> bus_width bar 
      1
exit [-force]

Exits SUE. Like the standard Tcl exit procedure but queries the user if there are modified cells before actually exiting. The -force argument bypasses the query as does setting BATCH to 1.

menu_add -menu (file|edit|view|sim|help) -label <name>
-command <command> -hotkey <hotkey> -help <string>

Adds the menu item <name> to the bottom of the given SUE menus. <command> is executed when the user hits this menu option. The <string> help line will be displayed in the message window when the user has the cursor over the menu option. If the label <name> is "separator", then a separator line will be added to the menu.

Example: 

      menu_add -menu file -label separator 
      menu_add -menu file -label foo -command "puts foo" -help "yippee!" 
     

SUE will not permit multiple menu entries with the same name. If the menu item has the same name as one on the same menu, it will be replaced, otherwise you will get an error.

unique_name <prefix> <primary_name> <secondary_name>

Returns a unique name that is guaranteed to be shorter than the size set by the global variable NETLIST_MAX_NAME_LENGTH. Note that SUE will reset NETLIST_MAX_NAME_LENGTH when netlisting depending on the netlisting mode. The name will start with the character <prefix>. The root of the name will be formed from <primary_name> if it is non-nil. Otherwise it will be formed from <secondary_name>. This procedure uses the global variable NAMES. During netlisting, NAMES will be reset for each schematic.

Example: 

      sue> unique_name "" foo bar 
      foo 
      sue> unique_name "" foo bar 
      foo_1

An API Example

Below is a short procedure called what that displays connectivity and net information about the current schematic. To use this procedure, you must either netlist (for instance, api_netlist) the schematic or generate terminal names (such as api_generate_term_names) first. You can add api_generate_term_names to the beginning of the procedure if you want but it may be redundant (or slow) if you have already netlisted. 

      proc what {} { 
        # first walk thru all of the instances 
        foreach id [api_types instance] { 
       
      	# figure out the type of this instance 
      	set data [api_instance_data $id] 
      	set type [get_assoc type $data] 
       
      	# get all of the ports on this instance 
      	foreach port_list [api_terminal_data $type] { 
      		set port [lindex $port_list 0] 
      		# could get the direction, too 
       
      		set net [api_netlist_data $id $port] 
       
      		if {$net == 0} { 
      			# can't find terminal, probably $name, need to lookup 
      			# clean up name. 
      			regsub -all {\{|\}|\$} $port "" port 
      			set port [get_assoc _$port $data] 
       
      			set net [api_netlist_data $id $port] 
      			if {$net == 0} {
			 puts "WARNING: can't determine net on port $port of type 
			 $type." 
      				 continue 
      			} 
      		} 
      		# save away in an associative array 
      		lappend nets($net) [list $type $port] 
      	} 
      } 
       
      # now walk thru all of the wires and get nets 
      foreach id [api_types wire] { 
       
      	set data [api_get_data $id] 
      	set net [get_assoc net $data] 
       
      	# save away in an associative array 
      	lappend nets($net) [list wire [get_assoc coords $data]] 
      } 
       
      # now show the user  
      foreach net [lsort -dictionary [array names nets]] { 
      	puts "$net: $nets($net)" 
      	} 
       
      	puts done 
      } 
     

To try out this example, cut and paste it into either a .suerc file or a file with the suffix .tcl. Bring up a schematic and netlist it. then type "what" on the SUE command line.

Additional API examples are found in the sample mmi_local (mmi_local.sample) directory included with each software release. Look in mmi_local.sample/sue/.suerc to see how to use these.
